title: Khronos Cameras through camera 0 -- the perspective one of the two the file puts at the same point

criterion.says: Two cameras and a simple plane mesh; a perspective camera and an orthographic camera.
criterion.note: Numeric because the whole of the criterion is which projection the plane is read through: the two cameras sit on two nodes at the same point and differ in nothing else, so a reader that adopted the wrong one draws a different silhouette of the same square in the same frame.

subjects.name: Cameras
subjects.notes: One mesh-bearing node, unnamed, carrying a unit square with no NORMAL and no material, plus two camera nodes at translation (0.5, 0.5, 3.0). THE FILE IS THE FIRST HERE THAT CARRIES MORE THAN ONE CAMERA, which is what it is for: `cameras[0]` is perspective at yfov 0.7 and `cameras[1]` is orthographic at xmag = ymag = 1, and no property of the scene distinguishes them but the projection.

source.pinReason: the same pin every other Khronos subject in this tree carries

blender.note: A release version, not a commit. Recorded so a red rung can be attributed to our renderer or to the oracle, and carried in the oracle's cache key so a version bump misses instead of serving a stale render. We do not aim to be bit-identical with Cycles.

camera.note: THE INDEX IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS CASE. Both sides resolve `cameras[0]` and neither takes whichever camera it met first: ours through Gltf::DeclaredPlacement, which requires exactly one node to reference the index, and the oracle's by matching the imported camera against the declaration Blender's importer built it from. The file states `aspectRatio: 1.0` and NEITHER SIDE APPLIES IT -- the frame the picture lands in decides the horizontal extent, because dividing by the file's number in a 16:9 frame scales x and y differently and turns a circle into an ellipse. Blender's importer drops it too (blender/imp/camera.py, 5.2.0, `# TODO: fov/aspect ratio`), so the agreement here is a real one and not two errors cancelling.

light.note: The only illumination is Blender's factory world. A uniform environment is what makes a Lambertian facet return rho*L with no integration left.

world.note: Configured by not being configured. The observed colour and strength go into provenance.json, so a Blender that changed them is visible without any machinery that refuses.

material.note: The subject is ONE unoccluded facet, which is the one shape where Cycles has no integration left and the answer is the closed form rho*L = 0.8 x 0.05087608844041824 = 0.0407008707523346. The mesh names no material at all, so declaring one here takes nothing away from the asset: what it tests is which of two projections the square is read through, and a colour cannot answer that. `diffuse` and not `emission` because there is no self-occlusion to remove, and the emission arm keys its colours on node names while this file's mesh node carries none.

default.note: One sample per pixel with the box filter at its RNA minimum makes Cycles evaluate the same predicate a centre-sampling rasteriser does, because the integer raster coordinate is the pixel centre and the sample never leaves +/-0.005 px of it.

notes: Its sibling `render/coverage/cameras-orthographic` renders the same file through `cameras[1]`, and the pair is the criterion: one subject, one manifest each, and the only difference between them is the index. THE FILE'S QUATERNION IS NOT UNIT -- (-0.383, 0, 0, 0.92375) has |q|^2 = 1.0000030625 -- and the format defines `rotation` as a unit quaternion, so the reader normalises it before building the matrix (src/gltf/Transform.cpp). Without that the same formula returns the rotation times |q|^2, which is 3.06 ppm of scale the node never declared. THIS CASE IS RED AT ONE PIXEL AND THE PIXEL IS ATTRIBUTED AS FAR AS AN INSTRUMENT REACHES: the oracle covers (502, 336) and we do not, that centre lies 0.00056 px from a projected edge, and the two hypotheses that could be tested were both refuted -- the quaternion is normalised on our side and the pixel stayed, and the oracle's coverage is bit-identical across two seeds so Cycles' 0.005 px box filter did not flip it. What is left is a sub-milli-pixel difference between two raster pipelines, and separating them needs an instrument that reads our own edge position on the GPU. It is the same signature as the other coverage residuals in this suite, whose disagreeing pixels all sit within 0.0013 px of an edge.

subjectFrameFraction.derivation: the sum over the subject's two triangles of the magnitude of the projected signed area, over 1280*720 at the file's camera 0, recomputed by the runner from the fetched vertices
subjectFrameFraction.note: What the boundary bound is applied UNDER: I.26's IoU ~ 1 - P*d/A makes P/A a property of the subject's size, so a camera that framed the subject smaller would tighten the bound without saying so. It is also what separates this case from its orthographic sibling: the same square through the other projection covers a different fraction of a different frame.
